description: Design, analyze and apply digital IIR and FIR filters. Covers classic analog-prototype designs (Butterworth, Chebyshev, elliptic), FIR windowing and equiripple methods, order-selection helpers, filter-structure conversions, response analysis and the one-line filtering functions.

tools.name: designfilt
tools.description: Modern, specification-driven filter designer that returns a digitalFilter object. You describe the response type ('lowpassfir', 'bandpassiir', ...) and give name/value specifications such as passband frequency, stopband attenuation and sample rate, and MATLAB picks a design method that meets them. Preferred over butter/fir1 for new code because the returned object carries its own specifications and works with filter, filtfilt, freqz and fvtool.
tools.usage: d = designfilt(respType, Name, Value, ...)

parameters.name: FilterOrder
parameters.description: Fixed filter order. Omit to let MATLAB choose the minimum order that meets the specs.

parameters.name: PassbandFrequency / StopbandFrequency
parameters.description: Band edges in Hz (when SampleRate is given) or in normalized units of pi rad/sample.

parameters.name: PassbandRipple / StopbandAttenuation
parameters.description: Allowed ripple and attenuation in dB.

parameters.name: SampleRate
parameters.description: Sample rate in Hz; makes all frequency specifications physical.

tools.notes: Call filtord(d), isstable(d) and fvtool(d) to inspect the result. designfilt with no output arguments opens an interactive design assistant.

tools.name: butter
tools.description: Design a Butterworth IIR filter, which has a maximally flat magnitude response in the passband and no ripple anywhere. Returns transfer-function coefficients [b,a], zero-pole-gain [z,p,k] or a state-space model depending on the number of outputs. Use it when passband flatness matters more than transition-band sharpness.
tools.usage:
[b,a] = butter(n, Wn)
[b,a] = butter(n, Wn, ftype)
[z,p,k] = butter(n, Wn, ftype)
[b,a] = butter(n, Wn, 's')

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Filter order. For bandpass/bandstop the resulting order is 2*n.

parameters.name: Wn
parameters.description: Cutoff frequency normalized so that 1.0 is the Nyquist rate (fs/2). Two-element vector for bandpass/bandstop.

parameters.name: 's'
parameters.description: Design an analog filter instead of a digital one.

tools.notes: For orders above about 6 prefer the [z,p,k] plus zp2sos route: direct [b,a] coefficients suffer badly from numerical round-off. Use buttord to pick n and Wn from specifications.

tools.name: cheby1
tools.description: Design a Chebyshev Type I IIR filter, which has equiripple in the passband and a monotonic stopband. For a given order it rolls off faster than a Butterworth filter, at the cost of passband ripple. Use it when you need a sharp transition and can tolerate a specified amount of passband ripple.
tools.usage:
[b,a] = cheby1(n, Rp, Wp)
[z,p,k] = cheby1(n, Rp, Wp, ftype)

parameters.name: Rp
parameters.description: Peak-to-peak passband ripple in dB, e.g. 0.5.

parameters.name: Wp
parameters.description: Passband edge frequency normalized to Nyquist; two elements for bandpass/bandstop.

tools.notes: cheb1ord returns the minimum order and the corresponding Wp for a given specification. Group delay is far less flat than for Butterworth, so use filtfilt when phase distortion matters.

tools.name: cheby2
tools.description: Design a Chebyshev Type II (inverse Chebyshev) IIR filter, with a monotonic passband and equiripple stopband. Because the passband is flat it distorts the wanted band less than Type I while still giving a steep transition. The stopband contains finite transmission zeros, so attenuation is guaranteed rather than monotonically increasing.
tools.usage:
[b,a] = cheby2(n, Rs, Ws)
[z,p,k] = cheby2(n, Rs, Ws, ftype)

parameters.name: Rs
parameters.description: Stopband attenuation in dB measured down from the peak passband value.

parameters.name: Ws
parameters.description: Stopband edge frequency normalized to Nyquist.

tools.notes: Note that Ws is the stopband edge, not the passband edge, which is the most common source of confusion. Use cheb2ord to choose n and Ws.

tools.name: ellip
tools.description: Design an elliptic (Cauer) IIR filter with equiripple in both passband and stopband. For a given order this gives the narrowest possible transition band of any classic design, which makes it the usual choice for sharp anti-alias and decimation filters. The price is strongly nonlinear phase and high sensitivity to coefficient quantization.
tools.usage:
[b,a] = ellip(n, Rp, Rs, Wp)
[z,p,k] = ellip(n, Rp, Rs, Wp, ftype)
tools.notes: Always implement elliptic designs as second-order sections. Use ellipord for automatic order selection.

tools.name: besself
tools.description: Design an analog Bessel filter, which has a maximally flat group delay and therefore preserves waveform shape in the passband. Because the Bessel property is only meaningful in continuous time, besself designs analog filters only; discretize with c2d or use an equivalent digital approach. Use it for pulse and step signals where overshoot and ringing must be minimized.
tools.usage:
[b,a] = besself(n, Wo)
[z,p,k] = besself(n, Wo, ftype)

parameters.name: Wo
parameters.description: Cutoff angular frequency in rad/s (analog, not normalized).

tools.notes: besself cannot produce digital filters directly. Combine with bilinear or impinvar, or use Control System Toolbox c2d.

tools.name: buttord
tools.description: Compute the lowest Butterworth filter order that meets passband and stopband specifications, together with the natural cutoff frequency to pass to butter. Takes band edges normalized to Nyquist plus the allowed passband ripple and required stopband attenuation. Use it so you never have to guess a filter order.
tools.usage:
[n, Wn] = buttord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
[n, Wn] = buttord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs, 's')
tools.notes: cheb1ord, cheb2ord and ellipord have identical calling syntax for the other prototypes.

tools.name: cheb1ord
tools.description: Return the minimum Chebyshev Type I order and passband edge frequency that satisfy given ripple and attenuation requirements. Its outputs feed directly into cheby1. Use it together with cheby1 whenever the design is specified by band edges and dB requirements rather than by order.
tools.usage: [n, Wp] = cheb1ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
tools.notes: Compare the orders returned by buttord, cheb1ord, cheb2ord and ellipord to choose a prototype family.

tools.name: cheb2ord
tools.description: Return the minimum Chebyshev Type II order and the stopband edge to use with cheby2. Signature matches buttord but the second output is a stopband rather than a passband frequency. Use it when you want a flat passband with a guaranteed stopband floor.
tools.usage: [n, Ws] = cheb2ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)

tools.name: ellipord
tools.description: Return the lowest elliptic filter order and passband edge that meet the given ripple and attenuation specifications. Because elliptic filters are the most selective classic design, the order it reports is usually the smallest of all four ord functions. Feed its outputs straight into ellip.
tools.usage: [n, Wp] = ellipord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)

tools.name: fir1
tools.description: Design a linear-phase FIR filter by the windowed-sinc method. You give the order and the normalized cutoff frequency, and fir1 multiplies the ideal impulse response by a window (Hamming by default). This is the quickest way to get a well-behaved, guaranteed-stable linear-phase FIR filter.
tools.usage:
b = fir1(n, Wn)
b = fir1(n, Wn, ftype)
b = fir1(n, Wn, window)
b = fir1(n, Wn, ftype, window, 'noscale')

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Filter order; the filter has n+1 taps.

parameters.name: Wn
parameters.description: Cutoff frequency (or vector of band edges) normalized to Nyquist.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Column vector of n+1 window values, e.g. kaiser(n+1, 5). Defaults to hamming(n+1).

tools.notes: High-pass and band-stop designs require an even order; fir1 increments an odd order and warns. Use kaiserord to compute n and the Kaiser beta from a dB specification.

tools.name: fir2
tools.description: Design an FIR filter with an arbitrary piecewise-linear magnitude response specified by frequency/amplitude breakpoint vectors. It interpolates the requested response onto a dense grid, takes an inverse FFT and applies a window. Use it for shaping, equalization or matching a measured response that no standard prototype fits.
tools.usage:
b = fir2(n, f, m)
b = fir2(n, f, m, window)
b = fir2(n, f, m, npt, lap, window)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Monotonically increasing frequency points from 0 to 1 (1 = Nyquist).

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Desired magnitude at each frequency in f.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window of length n+1; Hamming by default.

tools.notes: Duplicate a frequency value to create a step in the desired response. For equiripple optimal designs use firpm instead.

tools.name: firpm
tools.description: Design an optimal equiripple linear-phase FIR filter with the Parks-McClellan (Remez exchange) algorithm. It minimizes the maximum weighted error between the desired and actual response, so for a given order it gives the best possible stopband attenuation. Also supports differentiator and Hilbert transformer designs.
tools.usage:
b = firpm(n, f, a)
b = firpm(n, f, a, w)
b = firpm(n, f, a, 'hilbert')
b = firpm(n, f, a, 'differentiator')

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Band-edge frequencies in pairs, normalized to Nyquist, in increasing order.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Desired amplitude at each band edge.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Weight per band; larger weight forces smaller error in that band.

tools.notes: Transition bands are 'don't care' regions and must not overlap. firpm can fail to converge for very narrow transitions; increase the order or use designfilt with 'equiripple'.

tools.name: firpmord
tools.description: Estimate the FIR order, normalized band edges, amplitudes and weights needed by firpm to meet a given ripple specification. You pass band edges in Hz, the desired amplitude in each band and the maximum allowable deviation in each band. Its four outputs can be passed straight to firpm.
tools.usage:
[n, fo, ao, w] = firpmord(f, a, dev)
[n, fo, ao, w] = firpmord(f, a, dev, fs)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Transition-band edge frequencies (one pair per transition).

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Desired amplitude in each band (1 for pass, 0 for stop).

parameters.name: dev
parameters.description: Maximum allowable deviation (linear, not dB) in each band.

parameters.name: fs
parameters.description: Sample rate; if omitted, f is normalized to Nyquist.

tools.notes: The estimate can be one or two orders low; check with freqz and bump n if the specification is not met.

tools.name: firls
tools.description: Design a linear-phase FIR filter that minimizes the integrated squared error between the actual and desired piecewise-linear response. Unlike firpm it minimizes total energy error rather than peak error, which gives less stopband ripple far from the transition but more near it. Use it when overall energy matching matters more than a worst-case bound.
tools.usage:
b = firls(n, f, a)
b = firls(n, f, a, w)
b = firls(n, f, a, 'hilbert')

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Band-edge frequency pairs normalized to Nyquist.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Desired amplitude at each band edge (linearly interpolated within a band).

tools.name: kaiserord
tools.description: Estimate the FIR order and Kaiser window beta parameter needed to meet a ripple specification, and return the band edges and amplitudes ready for fir1. Kaiser-window designs trade order against attenuation through a single beta parameter, which makes them easy to tune. Use it as the standard recipe for a windowed FIR filter with a dB specification.
tools.usage:
[n, Wn, beta, ftype] = kaiserord(f, a, dev)
[n, Wn, beta, ftype] = kaiserord(f, a, dev, fs)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Transition-band edges in Hz (or normalized if fs is omitted).

parameters.name: dev
parameters.description: Maximum deviation in each band, in linear units.

tools.notes: Always pass 'noscale' to fir1 with a kaiserord design so the band is not renormalized and the specification is preserved.

tools.name: sgolay
tools.description: Compute Savitzky-Golay FIR smoothing/differentiation filter coefficients of a given polynomial order and frame length. It returns the full projection matrix so you can apply exact polynomial fits at the signal edges as well as in the steady state. Use it when you need to smooth data while preserving peak height and width, or to estimate derivatives of noisy data.
tools.usage:
b = sgolay(order, framelen)
[b, g] = sgolay(order, framelen, weights)

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Polynomial order; must be less than framelen.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Optional weighting vector of length framelen for weighted least squares.

tools.notes: For plain smoothing sgolayfilt is simpler; use sgolay when you also need derivatives or custom edge handling.

tools.name: filter
tools.description: Apply a rational transfer-function (direct-form II transposed) filter to data, one sample at a time in causal order. Works for FIR filters (a = 1) and IIR filters alike, and can carry state between calls for streaming. This is the basic, real-time-realizable filtering primitive in MATLAB.
tools.usage:
y = filter(b, a, x)
y = filter(d, x)
[y, zf] = filter(b, a, x, zi)
y = filter(b, a, x, zi, dim)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Numerator and denominator coefficient vectors; a(1) must be nonzero.

parameters.name: zi / zf
parameters.description: Initial and final filter state, for processing a long signal in blocks.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension to filter along (default: first nonsingleton).

tools.notes: filter introduces phase distortion. Use filtfilt for zero-phase offline filtering.

tools.name: filtfilt
tools.description: Zero-phase digital filtering: runs the filter forward, reverses the result, runs it again and reverses back. The result has exactly zero phase distortion and a magnitude response that is the square of the designed one, so the effective attenuation doubles in dB and the effective order doubles. Use it for offline analysis where preserving feature timing matters.
tools.usage:
y = filtfilt(b, a, x)
y = filtfilt(sos, g, x)
y = filtfilt(d, x)

parameters.name: sos, g
parameters.description: Second-order-section matrix and overall gain (numerically preferable for IIR).

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input signal; must be longer than three times the filter order.

tools.notes: Cannot be used for real-time or causal processing. Remember that the achieved ripple/attenuation are not the designed ones: design for half the dB attenuation you need.

tools.name: fftfilt
tools.description: FIR filtering by the overlap-add method using FFTs, which is much faster than filter for long FIR filters and long signals. It only supports FIR filters (no denominator). Use it when a straight convolution with hundreds or thousands of taps becomes the bottleneck.
tools.usage:
y = fftfilt(b, x)
y = fftfilt(b, x, n)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input signal (columns filtered independently for matrices).

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: FFT length to use; MATLAB chooses an efficient one by default.

tools.notes: fftfilt and filter give the same result to within round-off for FIR filters.

tools.name: sosfilt
tools.description: Apply a cascade of second-order sections (biquads) to a signal. Second-order-section form is numerically far more robust than a single high-order transfer function, so this is the recommended way to run any IIR filter of order greater than about four. Pair it with zp2sos or tf2sos.
tools.usage:
y = sosfilt(sos, x)
y = sosfilt(sos, x, dim)

parameters.name: sos
parameters.description: L-by-6 matrix, each row [b0 b1 b2 a0 a1 a2] for one biquad.

tools.notes: zp2sos returns a separate scalar gain g; remember to apply it or pass sos with the gain folded into the first section.

tools.name: freqz
tools.description: Compute and plot the frequency response (magnitude and phase) of a digital filter. Called with no output arguments it draws a two-panel plot with magnitude in dB and unwrapped phase in degrees. This is the first thing to run after any filter design to confirm it meets the specification.
tools.usage:
[h, w] = freqz(b, a, n)
[h, f] = freqz(b, a, n, fs)
freqz(sos, n, fs)
freqz(d)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Filter coefficients, or an sos matrix, or a digitalFilter object.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of frequency points (default 512); use a power of two for speed.

parameters.name: fs
parameters.description: Sample rate; makes the frequency axis physical in Hz.

parameters.name: 'whole'
parameters.description: Evaluate over the whole unit circle (0 to 2*pi) instead of 0 to pi.

tools.notes: fvtool gives an interactive version with magnitude, phase, group delay, impulse response and pole-zero plots in one window.

tools.name: freqs
tools.description: Evaluate the frequency response of an analog (Laplace-domain) filter given its numerator and denominator polynomials in s. With no outputs it plots magnitude and phase on log-frequency axes. Use it to check analog prototypes from butter/cheby1/ellip/besself with the 's' option.
tools.usage:
h = freqs(b, a, w)
[h, w] = freqs(b, a, n)
freqs(b, a)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Analog numerator and denominator coefficients in descending powers of s.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Angular frequency vector in rad/s at which to evaluate.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of automatically chosen frequency points.

tools.name: impz
tools.description: Compute and plot the impulse response of a digital filter. With no output arguments it produces a stem plot; with outputs it returns the response and the corresponding sample times. Use it to check FIR tap shape, to judge IIR settling time, and to verify stability empirically.
tools.usage:
[h, t] = impz(b, a)
[h, t] = impz(b, a, n, fs)
impz(d)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Filter coefficients, sos matrix, or digitalFilter object.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of samples; if omitted, impz chooses enough to show the response decay.

parameters.name: fs
parameters.description: Sample rate, so the time axis is in seconds.

tools.notes: stepz gives the step response; impzlength returns the number of samples impz would choose.

tools.name: stepz
tools.description: Compute and plot the step response of a digital filter. Useful for judging overshoot, ringing and settling behaviour, which are often more intuitive than the impulse response. Called with no outputs it draws the plot directly.
tools.usage:
[h, t] = stepz(b, a)
[h, t] = stepz(b, a, n, fs)
stepz(d)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Filter coefficients, sos matrix, or digitalFilter object.

tools.name: grpdelay
tools.description: Compute the group delay of a digital filter, that is the negative derivative of phase with respect to frequency. A constant group delay means no phase distortion, which linear-phase FIR filters achieve exactly. Use it to quantify how much different frequency components are delayed by an IIR design.
tools.usage:
[gd, w] = grpdelay(b, a, n)
[gd, f] = grpdelay(b, a, n, fs)
grpdelay(d)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Filter coefficients, sos matrix, or digitalFilter object.

tools.name: phasez
tools.description: Compute the unwrapped phase response of a digital filter in radians. Unlike the phase returned by freqz it is continuous, which makes it easier to see linear-phase behaviour and to differentiate for group delay. Use phasedelay for the related phase-delay measure.
tools.usage:
[phi, w] = phasez(b, a, n)
[phi, f] = phasez(b, a, n, fs)
phasez(d)

parameters.name: b, a
parameters.description: Filter coefficients, sos matrix, or digitalFilter object.

tools.name: zplane
tools.description: Plot the poles and zeros of a digital filter relative to the unit circle. Zeros are drawn as circles and poles as crosses, with multiplicities annotated. Use it to check stability (all poles strictly inside the unit circle) and to see which zeros create stopband nulls.
tools.usage:
zplane(b, a)
zplane(z, p)
zplane(d)
[hz, hp, ht] = zplane(...)

parameters.name: z, p
parameters.description: Column vectors of zeros and poles.

tools.notes: Pass row vectors for [b,a] form and column vectors for [z,p] form; zplane distinguishes the two cases by orientation.

tools.name: zp2sos
tools.description: Convert zero-pole-gain form into a cascade of second-order sections plus an overall gain. Pole-zero pairing and section ordering are chosen to minimize numerical sensitivity, which is essential for high-order IIR filters. This is the standard bridge between a design function and sosfilt or filtfilt.
tools.usage:
[sos, g] = zp2sos(z, p, k)
sos = zp2sos(z, p, k)
[sos, g] = zp2sos(z, p, k, order, scale)

parameters.name: z, p, k
parameters.description: Zeros, poles and gain from butter/cheby1/cheby2/ellip with three outputs.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: 'up' (default, poles closest to origin first) or 'down'.

tools.notes: If you call it with one output, the gain is folded into the first section. With two outputs you must multiply by g yourself.

tools.name: tf2sos
tools.description: Convert transfer-function coefficients [b,a] into second-order-section form with an overall gain. Internally it finds the roots and calls zp2sos, so it inherits the same pairing and ordering options. Use it to rescue an existing high-order [b,a] design that is numerically ill-conditioned.
tools.usage:
[sos, g] = tf2sos(b, a)
[sos, g] = tf2sos(b, a, order, scale)
tools.notes: Root finding on a high-order polynomial is itself ill-conditioned; prefer designing directly in [z,p,k] form with zp2sos.

tools.name: sos2tf
tools.description: Expand a second-order-section matrix back into a single numerator/denominator pair. Useful for reporting, for interfacing with code that only accepts [b,a], or for symbolic analysis. Be aware that the expansion can lose accuracy for high-order filters.
tools.usage:
[b, a] = sos2tf(sos)
[b, a] = sos2tf(sos, g)

parameters.name: g
parameters.description: Optional overall gain to apply to the numerator.

tools.name: tf2zp
tools.description: Convert transfer-function coefficients to zero-pole-gain form by rooting the numerator and denominator polynomials. Use it to inspect where a filter's poles and zeros lie, to test stability, or as an intermediate step toward second-order sections. The companion zp2tf performs the reverse conversion.
tools.usage: [z, p, k] = tf2zp(b, a)

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Numerator coefficients (row vector, or matrix with one row per output for MIMO).

tools.notes: tf2zpk is the discrete-time-oriented variant and is generally preferred for digital filters.

tools.name: zp2tf
tools.description: Build numerator and denominator polynomial coefficients from zeros, poles and gain. It is the inverse of tf2zp and lets you construct filters by placing poles and zeros by hand (notches, resonators, comb filters). The resulting [b,a] can be used with filter, freqz and impz.
tools.usage: [b, a] = zp2tf(z, p, k)

tools.name: lowpass
tools.description: One-line lowpass filtering: designs a minimum-order filter that meets default specifications and applies it with zero phase distortion. Accepts a numeric vector, matrix or timetable and returns the filtered signal. Called with no output arguments it plots the original and filtered spectra along with the filter response.
tools.usage:
y = lowpass(x, fpass, fs)
y = lowpass(x, wpass)
[y, d] = lowpass(___, Name, Value)
lowpass(___)

parameters.name: fpass
parameters.description: Passband edge in Hz (requires fs) or normalized (0 to 1) as wpass.

parameters.name: Steepness
parameters.description: 0.5 to 1 (default 0.85); higher gives a sharper transition and a longer filter.

tools.notes: Ask for the second output d to reuse the designed digitalFilter. For repeated filtering in a loop, design once with designfilt instead.

tools.name: highpass
tools.description: One-line highpass filtering with an automatically designed minimum-order zero-phase filter. Frequently used to remove DC offset and slow baseline drift from sensor and biomedical data. Call it with no outputs to see a diagnostic plot of the spectra and filter response.
tools.usage:
y = highpass(x, fpass, fs)
[y, d] = highpass(___, Name, Value)

tools.name: bandpass
tools.description: One-line bandpass filtering between two frequencies using an automatically designed zero-phase filter. It is the quickest way to isolate a frequency band (for example an EEG rhythm or a machine vibration order) without designing a filter by hand. Returns the designed digitalFilter as an optional second output.
tools.usage:
y = bandpass(x, [f1 f2], fs)
[y, d] = bandpass(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: [f1 f2]
parameters.description: Lower and upper passband edges in Hz.

parameters.name: Steepness
parameters.description: Scalar or two-element vector for each transition band.

tools.name: bandstop
tools.description: One-line band-rejection (notch) filtering that removes a frequency band while passing everything else. The usual application is stripping mains interference at 50 or 60 Hz and its harmonics. Zero-phase filtering keeps the timing of transient features intact.
tools.usage:
y = bandstop(x, [f1 f2], fs)
[y, d] = bandstop(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: [f1 f2]
parameters.description: Lower and upper stopband edges in Hz.

tools.notes: A very narrow notch needs a high Steepness and a long filter. For a single tone, an IIR notch built with zp2tf or designfilt('bandstopiir') is cheaper.

tools.name: medfilt1
tools.description: One-dimensional median filter: replaces each sample with the median of a sliding window. Unlike a linear filter it removes impulsive spikes and salt-and-pepper noise without smearing step edges. Use it as a robust pre-processing step before linear filtering or peak detection.
tools.usage:
y = medfilt1(x)
y = medfilt1(x, n)
y = medfilt1(x, n, blksz, dim)
y = medfilt1(___, nanflag, padding)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Window length (default 3). Odd values keep the output aligned with the input.

tools.notes: medfilt2 is the two-dimensional image equivalent in Image Processing Toolbox. Use 'truncate' padding to avoid artificial dips at the signal ends.

tools.name: sgolayfilt
tools.description: Apply a Savitzky-Golay polynomial smoothing filter to a signal. It fits a low-order polynomial to each sliding frame by least squares, which smooths noise while preserving the height and width of peaks far better than a moving average. Widely used for spectroscopy, chromatography and other peaky data.
tools.usage:
y = sgolayfilt(x, order, framelen)
y = sgolayfilt(x, order, framelen, weights, dim)

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Polynomial order, must be less than framelen.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Optional weight vector of length framelen.

tools.notes: A higher polynomial order preserves peaks better but rejects less noise. Compare against smoothdata(x,'sgolay',k) in base MATLAB.

tools.name: fvtool
tools.description: Open the Filter Visualization Tool, an interactive window showing magnitude, phase, group delay, impulse and step responses, pole-zero plot and coefficients for one or more filters. You can overlay several designs to compare them side by side. It is the standard way to sanity-check a filter design.
tools.usage:
fvtool(b, a)
fvtool(sos)
fvtool(d)
fvtool(b1, a1, b2, a2, ...)
hfvt = fvtool(___, 'Fs', fs)

parameters.name: b, a / sos / d
parameters.description: Coefficients, second-order sections, or digitalFilter objects to display.

parameters.name: 'Fs'
parameters.description: Sample rate so axes are labelled in Hz.

tools.notes: Requires a display; in headless batch jobs use freqz/impz/grpdelay instead.
